newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. seeks EU support for Internet framework.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks EU support for Internet framework.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley, carrying President Bill Clinton's proposal for an electronic free trade zone to Europe, said on Monday that governments should let the market decide on technical standards for the Internet.
Daley urged delegates at a conference attended by more than 40 government ministers to take the opportunity provided by the Internet to create the new trade zone without barriers.
"We have one option: to move forward as partners," he told a Global Information Networks conference sponsored by the European Union.

"To do less is to risk turning this next great economic stage into another dividing line among nations, where language, culture, geography, currency, history, and technology still keep us from working together."

Daley outlined the main points in Clinton's framework on doing business on the Internet. The president proposed last week that an agreement on creating a "free trade zone" on the Internet should be reached within a year within the context of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
After his speech, Daley told reporters that this did not mean that the United States would not tax transactions conducted over computer networks, but new barriers should not be erected.
"We do believe there should be no new taxes that discriminate against the Internet," he said. "Existing taxes, I would assume, would continue, as would sales tax."
Clinton's chief adviser on electronic commerce, Ira Magaziner, is travelling with Daley. After Bonn, Magaziner will visit Brussels and Asia to seek support for Washington's proposal.

The response to the idea in Europe was cool, but Daley said he thought Europeans were warming to the idea. "There will be a lot more in common with the Clinton framework than in disagreement," he said.
But Daley noted there were still deep differences between the United States and some European countries on issues such as encryption and online pornography.

Some European countries want to make internet service providers liable for the information carried on their computer networks. But Daley said the private sector should be encouraged to exercise self-control and ensure that personal data carried over networks could not be read or tampered with.
"We think the private sector should be encouraged to develop products that make consumers confident in using these systems," he said.
